01 — The Idea

Everyone was scared.
Nobody had an answer.

Every tool trying to answer "will AI take my job?" gave the same vague paragraph. No numbers. Nothing role-specific. Felt like a horoscope — true for everyone, useful for no one.

I wanted something that gave you a number. Your role, your tasks, your actual risk. That was the gap.

People don't need another think-piece about AI. They need a mirror.

The market wasn't hypothetical

Before writing a line of code, needed to know if the problem was measurable.

$10.4B
India edtech market in 2025
→ $30B by 2030 · 37M paying users
52%
of 18–24 yr olds worried about AI impact on careers
83%
of Indian workers willing to delegate work to AI
Anxious + engaged = ideal customer
22k+
employees hit by AI layoffs in early 2026 alone

Peer-reviewed research confirms AI anxiety directly increases willingness to pay for knowledge products. Lower self-efficacy = stronger payment intent. That's the TAM — academically validated, not vibes.

The competitive gap

Found 8+ global calculators. All free. All US/UK focused — USD pricing, Western jobs, zero LPA context. None built specifically for Indian working professionals. That gap was wide open.

02 — First Version & The Cost Problem

It worked.
Then the cost math hit.

One page, five questions, a score. Started on Claude API — quality was genuinely good, users could see themselves in the output. Then we ran the numbers at scale.

Users / monthClaude SonnetGemini 2.5 Flash
1,000₹250₹2510× cheaper
10,000₹2,500₹20010× cheaper
1,00,000₹25,000₹2,00010× cheaper

Claude: $3/$15 per million tokens. Gemini 2.5 Flash: $0.30/$2.50. One assessment = ~2,000 tokens. Decision made. Switched to Gemini — but commented the Claude code, never deleted it. Smart call. We eventually moved back to Claude once quality became the priority.

Don't delete the thing you're replacing. Comment it. You'll be glad you did.

Mid-testing we hit Gemini's free tier quota. 429 error, during a user session. Lesson: free tiers are for development, not demos. Always have billing set up before showing the product.

The domain problem

Started with 13 career domains. Every third real user fell outside them — supply chain analyst, legal associate, real estate consultant. Domain matching was failing. Expanded to 27. Not just more dropdown options — rebuilt the keyword matching logic and live job configs entirely.

03 — Breaking Into Pages

One page was doing
too many jobs.

Single-page version: quiz and results fighting for the same space. No progression. Split into three — /, /quiz, /results. Forced us to answer questions we'd been avoiding: what does each page actually do on its own?

The quiz

Five questions. Progress bar, input-validation microcopy, shake-animation instead of red error text — red errors feel like getting told off. Wrong energy for a product built around job anxiety.

Personalised entry — professional or student
Question 1 of 5 — progress bar, validation microcopy

The loading screen

API takes 8–12 seconds. First version: a spinner — users refreshed thinking it was broken. Replaced with rotating microcopy: "Scanning your role… Analyzing task patterns… Identifying pivots…" Same wait time. Felt intelligent. Drop-off stopped.

Loading screen — animated layers, rotating copy, progress percentage
04 — The Results Page

Delivering bad news
without losing the person.

The results page is the product. The challenge: show someone their score is 75/100 and have them still scroll down. Emotional arc: Anxiety → Understanding → Acceptance → Action. Every section placed with that sequence in mind.

Delivering bad news without making people feel hopeless — that's a product design problem, not a visual one.

The score reveal

Tried a full circle gauge first — confusing, no clear good/bad direction. Landed on a half-circle needle. Score counts up from 0, settles, risk badge fades in after. The animation isn't decoration. The score is the moment the user came for.

Score reveal — animated needle, risk badge, trust signals below
Reality Check — 3 role-specific signals, numbered for scanability

Live jobs & courses

First version returned irrelevant results — LLM engineer jobs for a real estate agent. Added domain validation, relevance scoring, keyword filtering, smart fallback to static data. Course ordering was wrong too: ₹66,000 as the first result killed momentum. Reordered by relevance, free options surfaced first.

Skills — ranked with inline market data citations
Career pivots — numbered with context
Live jobs — source badges, salary, skill tags
Live courses — relevance ordered, free options first
05 — The Design System

Warm, not clinical.
White is the call.

Explored dark mode seriously as the primary direction. Landed on white. Data consistently shows white performs better for reading-heavy, data-forward tools — when your product is a report someone has to actually process, dark mode adds cognitive friction. Dark mode is a future version feature, not a bolt-on.

One visual rule: warm, not clinical. Most tools in this space feel cold and threatening. We went the opposite direction.

#FAF9F7
Warm beige background — not stark white
#CC3320
Red accent — urgency without alarm
Sora 700
Headings — geometric, tight, confident
Sora 300
Body — light weight, long-form readable

Risk color system

Low (0–30): green. Moderate (31–55): amber. High (56–75): coral. Critical (76–100): red. The gauge gradient, risk badge, and table rows all use the same four colors. Severity communicated visually without spelling it out.

Landing — warm beige problem framing
Landing — dark contrast section within the white-primary page
06 — The Auth Decision

Login as a reward,
not a gate.

Looked at 16Personalities, Grammarly, Duolingo, LinkedIn Learning — all of them. Then looked at the actual data.

26%
abandon if forced to create account upfront
Baymard Institute, 2024
40–50%
account creation rate with OAuth vs 15–25% with password
+56%
form completion from removing the confirm password field alone

Every high-conversion product delays friction until after value lands. Login before score = gate. Login after payment = reward. Went login-wall-free until payment. No account to quiz, no account to see your score. OTP email only at payment — the highest-intent moment in the flow.

Paywall — only shows after score and reality check are visible
Razorpay — fully built and tested, awaiting live keys
07 — The Business Model

Flat pricing wasn't leaving
money on the table.
It was the whole table.

Started with flat ₹299. Ran the conversion math. Numbers were sobering.

65%
quiz start → completion rate
Interact 2026 · 80M+ leads
3–5%
B2C freemium → paid is considered "good"
ChartMogul 2026 · 200 SaaS cos.
6.5%
monthly churn for B2C subscriptions — why we ruled them out
Recurly 2025 · 1,200+ sites

Subscriptions don't work without retention infrastructure. Not there yet. One-time payment. And tiered pricing over flat:

+44%
Average revenue per user — tiered vs flat pricing
Price Intelligently · 1,000 SaaS companies
+30%
Mid-tier selection lift from the decoy effect (3 options vs 2)
ConversionXL

Free / ₹199 / ₹399. Free = score + reality check + blurred preview. ₹199 = full report. ₹399 = full report + 12 weekly digest emails with fresh jobs and AI news for your domain. Email as a dashboard — no extra auth complexity needed.

Paywall design: progressive teasing, not a blur wall. First skill fully visible. Second and third show the title with description blurred — users see exactly what they're buying. CTA: "Unlock My Full Plan · ₹99 · One-time · No subscription · Saved to your account." Every objection in one line.

Post-payment — user dashboard with snapshot and past assessments
08 — What We Got Wrong

The honest list.

  • 01
    Built too much before validating.

    Full payment flow, OTP auth, dashboard, PDF download — all before a single paying user. Architecture got complex before the core value was proven. Validate first, build infrastructure second.

  • 02
    The AI provider swap cost real time.

    Claude → Gemini → Claude. Two codebases in parallel for a while. Commenting rather than deleting was smart — but pick a provider and don't switch without a real reason.

  • 03
    429 error. Mid-demo. In front of users.

    Hit Gemini's free tier quota during a testing session. Free tiers are for development. Always have billing set up before showing the product to anyone.

  • 04
    Optimized before validating traffic.

    Built a full architecture optimization plan — Redis caching, streaming APIs, URL-addressable reports. All good ideas. All premature. Build for the stage you're in, not the stage you want to be in.

Built the payment modal before activating the keys. Full auth system before a single paying user. Same mistake, different clothes.

09 — Where It Is Now

It works.
Now it needs users.

Live at riskradar-vert.vercel.app. Quiz end-to-end, Claude API analysis, full results page — score gauge, reality check, skills, pivots, live jobs and courses. Next.js + MongoDB. OTP auth. Razorpay fully wired, awaiting live keys.

10 — What I Learned

The actual takeaways.

Emotional products need emotional design.

The gauge animation, the loading microcopy, the reality check opening with the user's actual job title — every decision that moved the needle was about how someone feels at a specific moment. Visual design is the surface. Emotional choreography is the work.

Copy is design.

"Scanning your role…" changed user behavior more than any visual change. "One-time · No subscription · Saved to your account" answered three objections in one line. The words are the design.

Data ends arguments.

The Baymard 26% stat ended the login-wall debate. The 6.5% churn number killed subscriptions. Data doesn't make decisions — it removes the opinion-based stalling that slows everything down.

Scope is a trap.

Build the thing that proves the value. Everything else is a bet without the information to make it well.

Distribution is the actual battle.

Not features, not polish. Getting found. Fifty SEO blog posts targeting "will AI replace [job] in India in 2026" — that's the unglamorous work that moves the needle. The product is ready.

The best thing we built wasn't the gauge animation or the live jobs API. It was making the score feel like a moment. Everything else is support.
